title: Milestone: One Web Page, Start to Finish
objective: After this level you can explain every step from typing a web address to seeing the page: bits, software, DNS, packets, servers and your browser.
summary: From Enter to pixels: DNS finds the server, a handshake connects, GET fetches the HTML, more requests fetch its files, and the browser lays out and paints the page.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one web page from Enter to screen.
cards.body: Your browser finds a server, asks for a page, collects the pieces and paints them onto your screen. You've now met almost every part of that trip. Here it is in order, from the key you press to the pixels you see.

events.label: DNS lookup: the site's name becomes the server's IP address
A TCP handshake opens a connection; HTTPS adds a TLS handshake
The browser sends a GET request, usually for the HTML
The HTML names style sheets, scripts and images: more requests
The browser builds the page's structure, styles and layout
Paint: every laid-out box becomes pixels on your screen

cards.headline: Every step leans on something you know
cards.body: The request and response are Level 41's, and a cookie reminds the forgetful server who you are. A nearby CDN copy trims the latency of each round trip, and JPEG compression keeps the photos small by dropping detail your eyes won't miss. At the very end, the browser converts each box into actual pixels: red, green and blue numbers from 0 to 255, straight out of Chapter 1.

cards.headline: Milestone: one page, end to end
learned: How a typed web address becomes a server's address, a connection and a request for the page.
Why the web forgets you between requests, and how cookies remind it who you are.
Why distance slows pages more than bandwidth, and how nearby copies and compression help.
How a browser turns HTML, CSS and JavaScript into the pixels on your screen.

questions.prompt: Why does the browser send several more requests after the first HTML file arrives?

options.label: The first request always fails and must be repeated
options.rationale: The first request usually succeeds; more files are needed.

options.label: The HTML names style sheets, scripts and images it still needs
Each request can only carry one word of the page
options.rationale: A response can carry a whole file.

options.label: The server asks the browser to send its cookies separately
options.rationale: Cookies ride along with each request.

questions.explanation: The HTML refers to other files (CSS, scripts, images), and the browser requests each one.

questions.prompt: What is the last step before you see the finished page?

options.label: The DNS lookup that finds the server
options.rationale: That's the very first step.

options.label: The TCP handshake that opens a connection
options.rationale: That happens early, before any request.

options.label: The GET request for the HTML file
options.rationale: That comes before the page is built.

options.label: Painting each laid-out box as pixels on the screen

questions.explanation: After layout, the browser paints: it converts each box into actual pixels on the screen.

questions.prompt: From Level 41: what does it mean that HTTP is stateless?

options.label: Nothing links one request to the next
Pages can be sent to any country without restrictions
options.rationale: Stateless is about memory, not borders.

options.label: Servers never send status codes
options.rationale: Every response carries a status code.

options.label: The browser keeps no copy of any page
options.rationale: It's about the server keeping no link between requests.

questions.explanation: HTTP keeps no link between two requests, so each must carry everything the server needs.

questions.prompt: From Level 43: how does a cookie keep you signed in as you move from page to page?

options.label: It stores your password on the server's screen
options.rationale: A cookie is data kept by your browser.

options.label: It makes the server remember every visitor forever
options.rationale: The server still forgets; the cookie reminds it.

options.label: The browser returns it with each request
It slows the requests down so they merge together
options.rationale: Requests stay separate; the cookie links them.

questions.explanation: The browser returns the cookie with later requests, letting the server tie them into one session.

questions.prompt: From Level 46: a much faster plan adds bandwidth. What does it leave unchanged?

options.label: How many bits it can move each second
options.rationale: That's bandwidth, which the plan increases.

options.label: How much data it can download in an hour
options.rationale: That grows with bandwidth.

options.label: The size of the pipe
options.rationale: The pipe's width is what bandwidth measures.

options.label: The delay set by the distance to the server

questions.explanation: Light in fiber needs time to cover the distance, about 28 ms from New York to London, whatever the bandwidth.

questions.prompt: From Level 47: why does a nearby CDN copy make a page load faster?

options.label: The request travels a much shorter distance
CDN servers use a different language than HTML
options.rationale: They serve the same files, just closer.

options.label: CDN copies have no images in them
options.rationale: The copies are the same files.

options.label: It skips the browser's layout and paint steps
options.rationale: The browser still builds and paints the page.

questions.explanation: A CDN answers each request from a server close to you, so each round trip is shorter.

questions.prompt: At the paint step, the browser sets every pixel. From Chapter 1, what is each pixel's color made of?

options.label: One letter code, such as ASCII 72
options.rationale: That's how text is stored, not a pixel's color.

options.label: A single bit that is either on or off
options.rationale: One bit gives only two options.

options.label: Red, green and blue values, each from 0 to 255
A tiny compressed JPEG of its own
options.rationale: The image is compressed, not each pixel.

questions.explanation: Each pixel mixes red, green and blue light, each a number from 0 to 255 that fits in one byte.
